paragraphs: Adaptive analysis lets later questions depend on earlier answers from the same dataset. The paper asks what kind of computational stability ensures that accurate answers about that sample also generalize beyond it. Its answer is a new stability notion defined through the information revealed by a computation's outputs.

Specifically, the notion measures how observing those outputs changes the posterior distribution over individual sample elements. This connects stability to what an observer can infer about the data after seeing the answers. The property survives post-processing and adaptive composition, so it remains applicable when outputs are transformed or computations are chosen using previous results.

The central result establishes necessity and sufficiency for computations answering bounded-sensitivity linear queries while maintaining sample accuracy. That scope is essential: the characterization concerns this specified class of computations. The paper also distinguishes its notion from earlier stability concepts and shows that every differentially private algorithm satisfies it, connecting an existing guarantee to this characterization of adaptive generalization.
neurips-2019-a-necessary-and-sufficient-.tldr: A new stability notion exactly characterizes adaptive generalization for sample-accurate computations answering bounded-sensitivity linear queries.

paragraphs: The paper investigates what makes machine learning research independently reproducible. Its starting point is that discussions often rely on intuition about good research practices rather than measurements of actual reproduction attempts. Releasing code matters, but the authors argue that code availability alone does not determine whether a paper can be independently reproduced.

To gather empirical evidence, they manually attempted to implement 255 papers published between 1984 and 2017. They recorded features of each paper and statistically analyzed the outcomes. This design connects characteristics of research reports with the practical experience of trying to implement their methods.

A defining choice was to avoid consulting the original authors' code, even when it was available. That kept implementation attempts from being guided by discrepancies between the paper and its accompanying software. The contribution described here is an empirical basis for studying independent reproducibility: it makes implementation attempts and paper characteristics the objects of measurement, rather than treating released code as a complete answer.
neurips-2019-a-step-toward-quantifying-i.tldr: Independent implementation attempts on 255 papers provide an empirical basis for studying what makes machine learning research reproducible.

paragraphs: Mixture models describe data using multiple components, but the names or ordering of those components need not have statistical meaning. Permuting their labels can leave the likelihood unchanged. During posterior inference, this symmetry creates label switching, which prevents standard Monte Carlo summaries from meaningfully tracking component-specific quantities.

The paper addresses the issue using optimal transport. Its algorithm computes posterior statistics in a quotient space of the symmetry group. In plain language, this means treating descriptions that differ only through the relevant symmetry as equivalent. The statistical summary is therefore organized around the underlying model rather than an arbitrary assignment of component labels.

The authors give conditions under which resolving label switching in this way has a meaningful solution. They also report advantages over alternative approaches on both simulated and real data. The approach matters because it incorporates the source of the ambiguity directly into posterior computation, while the stated conditions clarify that a meaningful resolution depends on the structure of the problem.
neurips-2019-alleviating-label-switching.tldr: An optimal-transport approach computes mixture-model posterior summaries while accounting for symmetries that cause label switching.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a common formulation for problems including convex minimization, convex-concave optimization, and nonatomic games. Fast methods for monotone deterministic problems typically rely on Lipschitz continuity, which controls how quickly the defining operator changes. Operators that become singular near the feasible region's boundary can violate this requirement.

The paper introduces Bregman smoothness as an alternative way to control operator variation. Instead of measuring that variation through the usual Lipschitz condition, it relates it to a suitably chosen Bregman function. This allows the analysis to reflect a geometry that can accommodate some boundary singularities.

Using this condition, the authors derive an adaptive Mirror-Prox algorithm with an O(1/T) convergence rate, where T counts iterations. The method does not require advance knowledge of the corresponding Bregman constant. The guarantee applies to problems satisfying the proposed condition, including possibly singular operators. A stochastic extension achieves O(1/√T), extending the framework to settings with randomness while providing a different convergence guarantee.
neurips-2019-an-adaptive-mirror-prox-met.tldr: Bregman smoothness enables adaptive Mirror-Prox convergence guarantees for problems whose operators may be singular at the boundary.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a pretrained network can be especially useful when the target task has little training data. However, retaining knowledge from the original task does not ensure that all of it helps the new task. This paper examines negative transfer, alongside the more commonly addressed problem of catastrophic forgetting.

Its empirical investigation finds that spectral components of both network weights and feature representations differ in transferability. These components provide a way to examine different directions within the learned parameters and representations. The finding motivates treating transferred information selectively rather than assuming its usefulness is uniform.

The proposed Batch Spectral Shrinkage method penalizes smaller singular values to suppress components identified as untransferable. It acts as a regularizer and can be added to existing fine-tuning methods. Experiments show significant improvements for representative methods, especially with limited training data. These results support the value of controlling which spectral components are retained during adaptation; they do not establish a universal guarantee that negative transfer disappears.
neurips-2019-catastrophic-forgetting-mee.tldr: Batch Spectral Shrinkage improves fine-tuning by penalizing smaller singular values to suppress poorly transferable components.

paragraphs: Learning a causal graph often involves matching conditional independences in data to constraints expressed by d-separation. This paper considers a broader setting with hidden variables and multiple observational and experimental distributions. Comparing these distributions can reveal invariances beyond the conditional independences used in conventional graph learning.

The authors connect these additional constraints to do-calculus under soft interventions. They define an interventional equivalence class that groups causal graphs according to the families of interventional distributions they permit. Two graphs are equivalent when the invariances obtained through direct application of the calculus rules cannot distinguish their associated distribution families.

The paper supplies a graphical representation and a formal characterization for deciding this equivalence. It also extends the FCI algorithm to combine observational and interventional datasets, adding orientation rules suited to this setting. Together, these contributions turn comparisons across distributions into information for causal structure learning, while explicitly representing cases in which the available invariances still leave multiple graphs indistinguishable.
neurips-2019-characterization-and-learni.tldr: The paper characterizes causal-graph equivalence under soft interventions and extends FCI to use observational and interventional invariances.

paragraphs: A single image can leave a person's three-dimensional pose ambiguous because depth is missing and body parts may be hidden. Multiple viewpoints provide geometric information for reconstruction, but their usefulness depends on what each camera can see. This paper focuses on choosing informative views in complex scenes containing multiple people.

ACTOR combines a two-dimensional pose estimator with a deep reinforcement learning policy that selects camera viewpoints. The policy also adapts the number of observations to the scene. Given an existing pose estimator, training the view-selection policy requires no annotations and proceeds through self-supervision.

Evaluations on scenes recorded from multiple viewpoints in a Panoptic dome show significantly more accurate three-dimensional reconstructions than strong multi-view baselines. The finding supports making view selection part of the learned reconstruction process. A separate proof-of-concept experiment indicates potential for connecting the policy to a physical drone observer; this is evidence of that possibility rather than a claim of fully demonstrated drone deployment.
neurips-2019-domes-to-drones-self-superv.tldr: ACTOR learns to select an adaptive number of informative camera views for more accurate multi-person 3D pose reconstruction.

paragraphs: Generalized zero-shot learning requires recognizing both previously seen classes and classes without training examples at test time. Semantic representations provide information about those unseen classes. The paper addresses the challenge of converting that information into useful visual features while preserving class meaning and distinctions between classes.

DASCN couples two generative adversarial networks in one framework. The primal network synthesizes visual features from semantic representations of seen and unseen classes, including representations reconstructed by the dual network. Its goal is to produce features that retain semantic information while separating different classes.

The dual network provides a complementary constraint: generated visual features should represent the prior semantic knowledge well. This makes the relationship between semantic descriptions and visual features an explicit part of adversarial learning. Experiments report significant improvements over the state-of-the-art approaches considered. The results support the proposed interaction between the two networks as a way to improve generalized zero-shot recognition while addressing semantic information loss during feature generation.
neurips-2019-dual-adversarial-semantics-.tldr: DASCN couples two adversarial networks to generate class-distinguishing visual features that preserve semantic knowledge for generalized zero-shot learning.

paragraphs: Some theoretical bounds on neural-network generalization depend on several measures of weight size, including Frobenius and spectral norms. This paper conjectures that jointly constraining these quantities during training could bring empirical errors closer to those bounds and improve accuracy. That motivation is a conjecture, rather than an established consequence of the bounds.

The method first normalizes weights according to different norms, then reparameterizes them so their norms have constant, finite upper bounds. This separates constructing suitably constrained weights from learning with them. Multiple constraints are represented through joint weight spaces, or manifolds.

The authors introduce fine-grained stochastic gradient descent, FG-SGD, to optimize on these manifolds, with an assurance of convergence to minima. Image-classification experiments show that applying FG-SGD to collections of manifolds defined by multiple constraints can improve baseline networks' accuracy. The empirical finding supports the usefulness of the training method, while remaining distinct from the motivating conjecture about closeness to theoretical generalization bounds.
neurips-2019-fine-grained-optimization-o.tldr: FG-SGD trains neural networks on weight manifolds with multiple norm constraints and improves image-classification accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Maximum likelihood estimation has attractive statistical properties, including asymptotic efficiency. But evaluating a model's likelihood can require a normalization term that is computationally intractable. This paper develops an alternative estimator intended to retain strong statistical guarantees while enabling inference for such models.

The Discriminative Likelihood Estimator, or DLE, comes from minimizing Kullback-Leibler divergence using density-ratio estimation and a Stein operator. These ingredients provide the proposed route to estimation when ordinary likelihood calculation is problematic. The authors also derive a dual formulation that makes the resulting optimization easier to carry out.

The analysis proves consistency and shows that, under mild regularity conditions, DLE's asymptotic variance can attain the efficiency bound. This is a conditional large-sample result, rather than a promise of optimal accuracy for every dataset. Numerical studies support the asymptotic theory, and an example successfully estimates an intractable model built using a pretrained deep neural network. Together, the theory and example connect statistical efficiency with inference in models whose likelihood is difficult to compute.
neurips-2019-fisher-efficient-inference-.tldr: DLE enables inference for intractable models and can attain asymptotic statistical efficiency under mild regularity conditions.

paragraphs: Accelerated optimization can move toward a fitted solution faster, but learning also depends on how that movement affects prediction error. This paper studies that distinction for linear least-squares problems in Hilbert spaces. It examines the implicit regularization produced by Nesterov acceleration and a variant of the heavy-ball method.

The authors derive learning-error bounds for these accelerated dynamics. Their results show faster decay of bias than ordinary gradient descent, together with more unstable behavior. The two effects matter jointly: reducing one source of error faster does not by itself establish better overall learning accuracy.

Consequently, the paper argues that acceleration should not generally be expected to improve accuracy over gradient descent. Its benefit can instead be reaching the same accuracy with less computation. Numerical simulations validate the theoretical results. The analysis uses polynomials induced by the optimization dynamics, spectral techniques, and concentration inequalities to connect the behavior of the iterative algorithms with their statistical learning properties.
neurips-2019-implicit-regularization-of-.tldr: For linear least-squares learning, acceleration can reach comparable accuracy with less computation without generally improving accuracy itself.

paragraphs: The paper asks what it means for a trained neural network to regard two inputs as similar. Its definition focuses on their coupled response to parameter changes: if a change intended to alter the output for one input also alters the other, the network has difficulty treating them independently.

The authors analyze the mathematical properties of this similarity measure and use it for low-complexity sample-density estimation. They also propose incorporating it into training so that examples known to be similar are treated as similar by the network. This makes the measure useful both for examining a trained model and for shaping its behavior.

The paper then uses this perspective to study self-denoising in regression with noisy labels. A multimodal image-registration task achieves nearly perfect accuracy despite label noise, which the authors explain through averaging across labels of similar examples. Retrieving samples the network perceives as similar also lets them quantify the denoising effect without access to true labels.
neurips-2019-input-similarity-from-the-n.tldr: A similarity measure based on shared responses to parameter changes helps analyze neural networks and explain self-denoising from noisy labels.

paragraphs: The paper studies networks generated from hidden points on a Euclidean sphere. Each node corresponds to a latent position, and the probability of an edge depends on the distance between two positions through an unknown link function. The task is to estimate those hidden pairwise distances from the graph.

The authors introduce a spectral estimator and an efficient algorithm for computing it. A central feature is that the algorithm does not require knowledge of the link function. This lets the method target the underlying geometry without first being supplied the rule that converts distances into connection probabilities.

The theoretical convergence rate matches the rate for nonparametric function estimation on the sphere, up to a logarithmic factor. The method can also consistently estimate the latent dimension. These results concern the stated spherical random-geometric-graph model: within that setting, they provide both a computational approach and statistical guarantees for recovering geometric information that is not directly visible in the observed network.
neurips-2019-latent-distance-estimation-.tldr: A spectral method estimates hidden spherical distances and latent dimension from graphs without knowing the connection-probability function.

paragraphs: Most sensorimotor learning starts with a fixed body and learns how to control it. This paper studies a different arrangement: simple agents learn both how to assemble larger bodies and how to coordinate those bodies' behavior. Body construction and control are therefore part of the same learning problem.

Each primitive agent is a limb with a motor at one end. A limb can initiate a connection to another nearby limb, attaching it magnetically to the parent's motor. The resulting composite can connect with further agents. As bodies become more complex, the control policy has an architecture that explicitly corresponds to the assembled morphology.

The authors evaluate these dynamic, modular agents in simulation. They report better generalization than static, monolithic baselines when either the environment or the agent's structure changes at test time. The findings support modular co-evolution as a way to improve adaptability in the evaluated settings, tying the organization of the controller to the body's changing structure.
neurips-2019-learning-to-control-self-as.tldr: Simulated modular limbs jointly learn self-assembly and control, improving generalization to changes in their environment and body structure.

paragraphs: In Stackelberg security games, a defender may learn about an attacker's unknown payoffs by observing responses to defensive commitments. This paper shows that such learning algorithms can be manipulated when the attacker responds untruthfully. The observations used for learning are themselves choices made by a strategic participant.

The authors find that manipulation normally leads the defender to learn a maximin strategy. Such a strategy can be computed without additional information about the attacker, so this outcome undermines the purpose of learning. The finding motivates explicitly accounting for how attackers may influence the information a defender receives.

The proposed response moves commitment to a higher level: the defender commits to a policy specifying how learned information determines the eventual strategy. The paper gives a polynomial-time algorithm for the optimal policy and a heuristic applicable even to infinite or completely unknown attacker payoff spaces. Empirical evaluation shows significant utility improvements compared with ignoring manipulation, supporting the value of designing the learning process around strategic responses.
neurips-2019-manipulating-a-learning-def.tldr: A defender can counter strategic manipulation of learning by committing to a policy governing how learned information changes its strategy.

paragraphs: Highly overparameterized neural networks make the choice of optimization algorithm important for understanding generalization. In a particular overparameterized regime, gradient-descent learning dynamics are governed by a kernel determined at initialization: the neural tangent kernel. This paper studies what preferences for learned functions arise in that regime.

The authors analyze the kernel and its associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. They focus on functions with finite norm in this space, studying smoothness, approximation, and stability. These properties address how functions vary, what they can represent, and how their behavior responds to changes in the input.

For convolutional networks, the analysis includes stability under image deformations. The paper also compares neural tangent kernels with other known kernels for similar architectures. Its contribution is a characterization of inductive bias through the function space associated with the training dynamics. The conclusions are situated in the specified kernel-governed regime, which is the setting that makes this mathematical view of neural-network learning applicable.
neurips-2019-on-the-inductive-bias-of-ne.tldr: The paper analyzes neural tangent kernel function spaces to characterize smoothness, approximation, and stability in a particular overparameterized learning regime.

paragraphs: Online learning repeatedly makes decisions as information arrives, and regret measures performance against a comparison strategy. This paper uses differential privacy tools to analyze that learning process. The motivating connection is algorithmic stability: methods developed to control sensitivity to information can also help control accumulated learning error.

The authors introduce one-step differential stability, a property designed for refined regret analysis. It yields bounds for problems including online convex and online linear optimization. The property is particularly useful for first-order regret bounds for follow-the-perturbed-leader algorithms, a form of analysis that earlier approaches had struggled to achieve.

The paper also extends max-divergence to a family called Tsallis max-divergences. These give stronger stability notions useful when the learner receives only partial information, including multi-armed bandits and bandits with experts. The contribution is therefore an analytical framework spanning different feedback settings: privacy-inspired measures of stability become tools for proving how well online decision-making algorithms perform.
neurips-2019-online-learning-via-the-dif.tldr: Privacy-inspired stability notions yield refined regret bounds for online learning with both full and partial feedback.

paragraphs: Differential privacy guarantees survive any post-processing of a mechanism's output. This paper asks a stronger question: under what conditions can randomized post-processing improve those guarantees? It represents post-processing as a Markov operator, connecting privacy amplification to the behavior of an associated stochastic process.

The authors first derive amplification results using uniform mixing properties. They then develop coupling-based bounds for cases where uniform mixing is unavailable. A further contribution is a family of diffusion-based mechanisms that remains closed under post-processing, with privacy analyzed through a heat-flow argument. These approaches provide different routes to establishing when amplification occurs.

For applications, the paper generalizes privacy-amplification-by-iteration analysis for Noisy SGD and obtains an exponential improvement in the strongly convex case. It also studies an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck diffusion mechanism containing the Gaussian mechanism with optimal post-processing on bounded inputs as a special case. The results make amplification conditional on mathematical properties of the process and problem, rather than claiming that every randomized transformation strengthens privacy.
neurips-2019-privacy-amplification-by-mi.tldr: Mixing, coupling, and diffusion analysis establish conditions under which randomized post-processing strengthens differential privacy.

paragraphs: Graph kernels traditionally measure similarity between whole graphs for classification. This paper adapts kernel methodology to classifying individual nodes, where representations need to capture structural information within a graph. Its aim is to provide a theoretical foundation for a setting the authors describe as heavily dependent on heuristics.

The proposed framework learns node representations through a kernel-based formulation. The authors theoretically establish that the formulation has the expressive power of any positive semidefinite kernel. For efficient learning, they introduce a node-feature aggregation mechanism together with a similarity metric learned from data during training.

The framework is also designed to complement graph-based deep learning models, including Graph Convolutional Networks. Evaluations on standard node-classification benchmarks report state-of-the-art results. The theoretical and empirical contributions address different aspects of the approach: the expressiveness result characterizes the formulation's capacity, while the benchmark findings show how the proposed learning mechanism performs on the evaluated node-classification problems. Together, they connect graph similarity methods with learned representations of individual nodes.
neurips-2019-rethinking-kernel-methods-f.tldr: A kernel-based framework learns structural node representations and reports state-of-the-art node-classification results.

paragraphs: The paper studies a multiplayer bandit problem motivated by cognitive radio networks. Several players choose arms simultaneously, and collisions occur when multiple players select the same arm. The central challenge is coordinating learning and choices when decisions are decentralized.

The proposed algorithm deliberately causes some collisions to communicate information between players. Under the standard model, this protocol has negligible cost and enables performance matching a centralized algorithm. The result contradicts existing lower bounds for that problem by exploiting a communication opportunity embedded in the model's collision behavior.

That observation motivates a different dynamic setting without sensing, where comparable collision-based communication protocols are no longer possible. The authors introduce another algorithm and show that regret can still grow logarithmically in this setting. The paper thus contributes both algorithms and a modeling lesson: whether collisions can carry usable information changes what decentralized learners can achieve, so communication possibilities must be reflected in the formulation of the problem.
neurips-2019-sic-mmab-synchronisation-in.tldr: Deliberate collisions enable centralized-level multiplayer bandit performance, motivating a no-sensing model that still permits logarithmic regret.

paragraphs: Stochastic Gradient Hamiltonian Monte Carlo methods use stochastic gradient information to sample from a target distribution. This paper focuses on reducing the variance of that information. It introduces SRVR-HMC, a Hamiltonian Monte Carlo algorithm built around a recursively variance-reduced gradient estimator.

The estimator is semi-stochastic and accumulates gradient information recursively. This accumulated information is used to reduce the variability of the stochastic gradient supplied to the sampling procedure. The contribution therefore links a change in gradient estimation to the convergence behavior of the overall sampler.

The authors analyze sampling from a class of non-log-concave distributions and establish faster convergence than existing HMC-type algorithms based on underdamped Langevin dynamics. The comparison is scoped to that algorithm family and the distribution class covered by the analysis. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theory and show advantages for SRVR-HMC. Together, these findings indicate that recursively retaining gradient information can improve both the analyzed convergence behavior and empirical performance of this sampling approach.
neurips-2019-stochastic-gradient-hamilto.tldr: SRVR-HMC recursively reduces gradient variance to accelerate sampling for a studied class of non-log-concave distributions.

paragraphs: Neurons in the primary visual cortex can be influenced by surrounding activity through a phenomenon called surround modulation. Inspired by this behavior, the paper adds excitatory and inhibitory connections between units and their neighbors in convolutional neural networks. These connections let nearby activity strengthen or suppress a unit's response.

Experiments show that this simple change can substantially improve visual-task performance and training speed in traditional CNNs. The authors also test visual challenges involving clutter and changing lighting conditions, reporting better generalization in these situations. The results connect the proposed local connectivity structure with practical changes in visual processing.

The study further examines activity statistics, including sparsity and decorrelation, to investigate how the altered connections affect internal representations. It reports several effects analogous to those associated with surround modulation in visual cortex. These observations provide insight into possible sources of the mechanism's efficiency, alongside the direct performance results, without establishing that the network reproduces every aspect of biological vision.
neurips-2019-surround-modulation-a-bio-i.tldr: Biologically inspired excitatory and inhibitory connections improve CNN performance, training speed, and generalization in evaluated visual challenges.

paragraphs: This paper starts from a practical view of domain similarity: a model trained on one domain should perform well on the other, and the relationship should work in both directions. It formalizes that intuition through a performance gap measuring discrepancy between source and target domains.

The authors derive generalization bounds for instance-weighted transfer learning, where training examples receive different weights. Their analysis interprets the performance gap as an algorithm-dependent regularizer that controls model complexity. This ties the usefulness of source data to the behavior of the learning algorithm, rather than treating domain discrepancy as entirely separate from the model being trained.

The resulting theory motivates general rules for designing instance-weighting schemes. Those rules lead to gapBoost, a boosting approach for transfer learning. Benchmark experiments show significant improvements over previous boosting-based transfer methods. The contribution combines a way to reason about transfer with a concrete algorithm: cross-domain performance helps guide how examples are weighted, and the evaluated implementation improves results within that comparison.
neurips-2019-transfer-learning-via-minim.tldr: A cross-domain performance-gap principle yields transfer-learning bounds and motivates gapBoost, which improves on evaluated boosting-based transfer methods.

paragraphs: A medoid is the member of a dataset with the smallest total distance to all other members. Computing every pairwise distance identifies it exactly but requires quadratic work in the number of points. Earlier randomized approaches reduce this burden by adaptively selecting distances to query through a multi-armed bandit formulation.

This paper goes beyond a direct conversion to a standard bandit problem. It modifies the sampling strategy to exploit the structure of medoid computation and combines that strategy with a suitably chosen bandit algorithm. The key idea is that the original computational problem contains structure that a generic sampling rule need not fully use.

On real data, the authors report gains of four to five orders of magnitude over exact computation in both distance evaluations and elapsed time. They also provide theoretical results expressing gains in terms of data parameters. The empirical speedups are therefore findings on the evaluated data, while the analysis describes how the benefits depend on properties of the underlying problem.
neurips-2019-ultra-fast-medoid-identific.tldr: A structure-aware bandit sampling strategy greatly accelerates medoid identification on evaluated real datasets.

paragraphs: ViLBERT learns representations that connect images and language before specializing in a particular downstream task. It extends BERT into a two-stream architecture: visual inputs and text are processed separately, while co-attentional transformer layers let the streams interact. This provides a shared model for learning relationships between the two input types.

The authors pretrain the model using two proxy tasks on the automatically collected Conceptual Captions dataset. They then transfer it to visual question answering, visual commonsense reasoning, referring expressions, and caption-based image retrieval. Only minor additions to the base architecture are needed for these different tasks.

The evaluations report significant improvements over existing task-specific models and state-of-the-art results on all four tasks. These findings support treating visual grounding—the connection between language and image content—as a capability that can be pretrained and transferred. The contribution is both architectural and methodological: interacting visual and textual streams are used to learn representations that serve several downstream purposes.
neurips-2019-vilbert-pretraining-task-ag.tldr: ViLBERT pretrains interacting visual and language streams that transfer successfully to four vision-and-language tasks.
